explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "Son of man, these men have set up idols in their hearts…" (Ezekiel 14:3). Son of man is the name the LORD uses when He speaks to Ezekiel. No shelf, no statue in the corner. This is about what they were holding closest on the inside.

I get the guess, friend. Idols and houses go together in most people's heads. But the LORD says the idols are set up "in their hearts" (Ezekiel 14:3). Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, is the one who hears it. So this is about the inside of the elders, not the furniture.

Hilltops are a fair guess, since idols did show up in high places elsewhere in the Bible. Not here, though. The LORD tells Ezekiel these men "have set up idols in their hearts" (Ezekiel 14:3). Nobody had to climb anything. The whole problem was sitting inside them.

Yes, baker! The LORD asks, "Should I consult with them in any way?" (Ezekiel 14:3). It's a question, and the elders are sitting right there in front of Ezekiel when He asks it. I think that question carries some weight. Keep it in your pocket, because the rest of the passage answers it.

Close, but the text says otherwise, friend. The LORD does ask Ezekiel: "Should I consult with them in any way?" (Ezekiel 14:3). He says it about the elders who had come and sat down. So the question is really in there. It's the first thing the LORD says to Ezekiel about them.

explanations.answer: To take hold of Israel's hearts
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The LORD says He will answer "so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel" (Ezekiel 14:5). The reason is stated right there in the verse. It's about their hearts, which is the same place the idols were sitting.

Good guess, since prophets do come up in this passage. But the LORD gives a different reason: "so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel" (Ezekiel 14:5). Nothing in that verse says it's about silencing anybody. It's about their hearts.

Easy one to reach for, friend. Ezekiel and the people around him are already living among the exiles. Still, the verse never gives exile as the reason. The LORD says He will answer "so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel" (Ezekiel 14:5).

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "For because of their idols, they are all estranged from Me" (Ezekiel 14:5). Notice the word "all." It's not a small group sitting in the corner. That's a big word to carry around.

The elders are the ones sitting in front of Ezekiel, so I see why you went there, friend. But the LORD widens it: "they are all estranged from Me" (Ezekiel 14:5). He's talking about the people of Israel, not just the men in the room. That one little word "all" changes the whole picture.

I can see the thinking, baker. It's tempting to hope it's just a few. But the LORD says, "For because of their idols, they are all estranged from Me" (Ezekiel 14:5). That's a lot more than a few. The word is "all."

Yes, baker! The LORD says, "Repent and turn away from your idols…" (Ezekiel 14:6). Repent means turning around, and the verse says it right next to turning away. After all that heavy talk, here is a door held wide open. I think that's good news worth stopping on.

I love the energy, friend, but that's not the word. The LORD says, "Repent and turn away from your idols…" (Ezekiel 14:6). Rejoicing is wonderful, but the first step here is turning around. Think of it like a wrong turn: you can't enjoy the view until you've turned the car.

Remembering is a fine thing, baker, and Scripture talks about it a lot. But in this verse the LORD says, "Repent and turn away from your idols…" (Ezekiel 14:6). He asks for a turning, not just a thought. The word is Repent.

That's right, baker. The LORD says it covers "any Israelite or any foreigner dwelling in Israel" (Ezekiel 14:7). A foreigner who lived among the people is named right there in the verse. The warning isn't only for one group.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "For when any Israelite or any foreigner dwelling in Israel separates himself from Me, sets up idols in his heart…" (Ezekiel 14:7). That includes the foreigner who lives in Israel. The verse names both.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "I will set My face against that man and make him a sign and a proverb…" (Ezekiel 14:8). A sign points at something, and a proverb gets repeated. People would hear about this man and remember it. It's a serious thing to be standing there when the LORD sets His face against you.

I see why, friend. Those words sound important, like something a man might hope to be. But the LORD says He will "make him a sign and a proverb" (Ezekiel 14:8). That's not a job title. It's something people would point to and talk about.

That sounds like a nice future, baker, and that's why it doesn't fit. The LORD says, "I will set My face against that man and make him a sign and a proverb" (Ezekiel 14:8). A sign and a proverb, not a priest and a guide. The verse is not handing out promotions.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "I will cut him off from among My people" (Ezekiel 14:8). That's a heavy line, and it's right there in the verse. Then the LORD says, "Then you will know that I am the LORD."

I get the hope, friend, but the text says it plainly. The LORD says, "I will cut him off from among My people" (Ezekiel 14:8). He says it about the man who came with idols in his heart. It's a hard verse, and the Bible doesn't soften it here.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "But if the prophet is enticed to speak a message, then it was I the LORD who enticed him…" (Ezekiel 14:9). That's a tough verse, and the text doesn't explain how it works. So I'll just leave it exactly as God says it.

The elders are the ones who came to ask, so I get it, friend. But the LORD says who enticed the prophet: "then it was I the LORD who enticed him…" (Ezekiel 14:9). The verse names the LORD, not the elders. It's a heavy one, and the text doesn't say more about how.

Good thinking, baker, since false prophets come up a lot in the Bible. But this verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, "But if the prophet is enticed to speak a message, then it was I the LORD who enticed him…" (Ezekiel 14:9). He names Himself as the one.

explanations.answer: Stretch out His hand against him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel" (Ezekiel 14:9). It's a heavy line, and it's good to just let it be heavy. I think this one hurts a little to read.

explanations.answer: Lift up His hand to bless him
explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but it doesn't. The LORD says, "I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel" (Ezekiel 14:9). His hand is stretched out against the prophet here, not lifted to bless. It's a heavy verse.

explanations.answer: Put new words in his mouth
explanations.explanation: That's a thing God does in other places, baker, so I see where it came from. But this verse says something else. The LORD says, "I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel" (Ezekiel 14:9). It's a hard one.

I see why you'd think so, baker, but the text says otherwise. The LORD says, "They will bear their punishment—the punishment of the inquirer will be the same as that of the prophet" (Ezekiel 14:10). The same, not lighter. It's a heavy verse, and the Bible doesn't water it down.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "the punishment of the inquirer will be the same as that of the prophet" (Ezekiel 14:10). The one who came asking and the prophet get the same. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

I understand the worry, friend, but it's the opposite. The LORD says it is "in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me…" (Ezekiel 14:11). He wants them to stop straying, not to stay far. After all the hard words, this verse points back toward Him.

That's right, baker. The LORD says it is "in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me and no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions" (Ezekiel 14:11). It's about drawing them back, not pushing them away. After a heavy stretch, that's a verse to breathe in.

Yes, baker! The LORD says, "Then they will be My people and I will be their God" (Ezekiel 14:11). After all those hard words, the passage ends right here. I think it's the best way it could have ended.

That's the one, friend. The LORD says, "Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD" (Ezekiel 14:11). It's the second half of that promise. After the idols and the warnings, He says this is where it's all going.

Guests is a warm word, baker, and I'd put out the good cookies for them. But the LORD says, "Then they will be My people and I will be their God" (Ezekiel 14:11). Guests come and go, and this promise is bigger than that. It's about belonging.

Neighbors are nice, friend, especially the ones who return your cookie plate. But that's not what the LORD says. He says, "Then they will be My people and I will be their God" (Ezekiel 14:11). That's a lot closer than neighbors.

I see why the word came up after such a serious passage, baker. But the verse closes differently. The LORD says, "Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD" (Ezekiel 14:11). It ends on belonging, not on a courtroom.
